name: Hyaluronic acid lip balm

lead: Hyaluronic acid lip balms add hyaluronic acid, a molecule that binds large amounts of water, to a conventional lip balm. The appearance payoff is smoother, softer, better-hydrated lips with less flaking, and a fuller look from improved hydration.

Lip balms in general work by forming a protective layer that keeps moisture in and shields lips from wind and cold. Hyaluronic acid is a common humectant ingredient in skin care because of its water-binding ability.

paras: It is applied to the lips as needed through the day or before bed, and sometimes under lip color. Some people layer it with an occlusive balm.

Generally low risk. Dermatologists note that some balm ingredients and fragrances may irritate sensitive lips. Hyaluronic acid used topically is not the same as injectable hyaluronic acid lip filler, which has its own risks.

chain: HA binds water at the lip surface
angle.text: People use it to keep lips hydrated and smooth, which helps them look healthier and a little fuller. It is a topical product and does not change lip volume the way filler does.

lead: A hyaluronic acid lip balm is a lip care product that includes hyaluronic acid (HA) alongside the waxes and emollients of a typical balm. Lip balm in general is a wax-like product that moisturizes and relieves dry or chapped lips by forming a protective layer that keeps moisture in.[1]

HA is a common skin care ingredient: its negative charge lets it bind water, which is linked to its value in cosmetics.[2] In a balm, the aim is lips that look smoother and more hydrated, and so slightly fuller, without the procedure of lip filler.
Hyaluronic acid was first isolated in 1934 by Karl Meyer and John Palmer from the vitreous of a cow's eye.[2]

paras: Common lip balm bases include beeswax, candelilla and carnauba wax, with ingredients such as lanolin, paraffin and petrolatum; some products add dyes, flavoring or sunscreen.[1] Hyaluronic acid is added as a humectant. In skin tissue, HA helps keep tissue hydrated, and the reference notes it is a common ingredient in skin care products.[2]

HA is also used as an injectable dermal filler, with effects lasting about 6 to 12 months; filler complications include bruising, redness and, rarely, vascular occlusion.[2] A topical balm is a different product.

Lip care from beeswax, olive oil and animal fat is reported from ancient Egypt; petroleum jelly was introduced in 1872, ChapStick was developed in the 1880s, Carmex was created in 1937 and the first flavored balm arrived in 1973.[1]

Experts note that some ingredients and fragrances in lip balms may irritate sensitive lips, and a 2015 German test found mineral oil hydrocarbons in some mineral-oil-based products, which prompted a watchdog warning.[1]

No studies found of hyaluronic acid lip balms specifically. A study funded by a lip balm maker reported hydration lasting about eight hours and improved lip barrier function with consistent use of a conventional balm.[1]
